card: Numerals decline too. In the nominative and inanimate accusative, the 1 / 2–4 / 5+ rule applies. In **every other case** the noun simply goes into the **plural of that case**, and the numeral agrees: **о двух кни́гах**, **с пятью́ друзья́ми**, **к трём часа́м**.

sections.body: The 1 / 2–4 / 5+ rule only applies when the whole phrase is nominative (or accusative of things). The moment the phrase needs another case because of a preposition or verb, the numeral itself takes that case and the noun follows in the plural of the same case. In other words, in the oblique cases Russian behaves the way an English speaker would expect.

sections.title: пять to два́дцать, три́дцать: like a feminine -ь noun

head: Case
table.caption: **сто** and **со́рок** have one oblique form each: **ста**, **сорока́**. **девяно́сто** has **девяно́ста**.

sections.title: Putting it together
sections.body:
- **nominative**: **два бра́та**, **пять бра́тьев** (the rule)
- **genitive**: **у двух бра́тьев**, **у пяти́ бра́тьев**
- **dative**: **к двум бра́тьям**, **к пяти́ бра́тьям**
- **accusative, animate**: **Я ви́жу двух бра́тьев.** (= genitive)
- **instrumental**: **с двумя́ бра́тьями**, **с пятью́ бра́тьями**
- **prepositional**: **о двух бра́тьях**, **о пяти́ бра́тьях**

In compound numbers every part declines in formal Russian: **с двадцатью́ пятью́ рубля́ми**. In speech people often simplify, but the formal rule is what you'll see written.

sections.title: Collective numerals: дво́е, тро́е
sections.body: With people (especially male or mixed groups), pluralia tantum and children, Russian often uses **дво́е, тро́е, че́тверо** + genitive plural: **дво́е дете́й**, **тро́е су́ток**, **Нас бы́ло че́тверо.** (*There were four of us.*) **о́ба / о́бе** (*both*) follow the 2–4 rule: **о́ба бра́та**, **о́бе сестры́**.

mistakes.why: After **с** both numeral and noun go into the instrumental plural.

examples.en: He came back five days later.
